You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Science and Technology for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course. Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the
book's own terms and spellings.
Course: "10. Tissues and Its Types" · subject: Science and Technology · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.

Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a question or an answer option is a role, not a type. BIE's code proposes a type before you read the page; when you choose another, say why. The content type decides the required questions and later how the lesson teaches it, how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.
[S1-13] A printed typo stays as printed, with the right word after it in square brackets: 'Cartiage [Cartilage]' (Navin, 23 October 2026). The teacher answers use the right word. Never correct the book silently.
[S1-14] One answer, one basis (Navin, 23 October 2026): an answer that would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one with basis 'book' (only what the page states) and one with basis 'outside'.
[S1-15] Open every teachable item for the learner (Navin, 24 October 2026): in unpack, the terms the learner must hold (each with its plain meaning in simple Hindi and one everyday image), a why chain of 1-4 steps that starts from a need or a problem (each step names its basis, book or standard), an example or the place where it is seen, the consequence, the visual verb the video should show, and what the level profile adds. Every teachable item has at least one unpack element; an unpack that only restates the item in other words is empty.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;
    BIE's code sends an item back for a textbook translation. For example "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"),
    everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-24.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.

items.content: Q. …………… layer is thickest and helps in protection against water loss and further secrete [secretes] a waxy substance on outer surface:

teacher_understanding.question: What combination of clues is the question testing?
teacher_understanding.answer: The stem combines a layer described as 'thickest', protection against water loss and secretion of a waxy substance on the outer surface.

teacher_understanding.question: Which option is intended?
teacher_understanding.answer: Option b, Epidermis, fits the protective outer covering and waxy secretion clues. No answer is marked on this page.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this covering situated?
teacher_understanding.answer: The epidermis forms the outer covering of primary plant organs; on many aerial parts its outer surface bears a cuticle.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the waxy covering reduce water loss?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cuticle forms a water-resistant barrier, reducing evaporation through the exposed surface.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should 'thickest' not be memorised as a general property of epidermis?
teacher_understanding.answer: Epidermis is commonly a single cell layer. Its thickness and the thickness of its cuticle vary with the organ and environment; it is not generally the thickest plant tissue layer.

prerequisites: plant organs have an outer covering
water can evaporate from exposed surfaces
items.exam_note: Intended answer: b. Use the function clues; flag rather than endorse the unqualified word 'thickest'.

teacher_understanding.question: What is sclerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a supporting plant tissue whose mature cells usually have thick, lignified walls and lack living contents.

teacher_understanding.question: Where can its support function be recognised?
teacher_understanding.answer: Coconut husk fibres and hard seed coverings are familiar examples of sclerenchymatous support.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a thick wall not enough to make this the correct answer?
teacher_understanding.answer: Thick lignified walls provide strength; the stem asks for an outer covering that produces a waxy barrier against water loss, which points to epidermis.

items.exam_note: Distractor exploits the word 'thickest'; distinguish mechanical strength from surface waterproofing.

terms.plain_meaning: पौधे का सहारा देने वाला tissue, जिसकी cell walls मोटी और कड़ी होती हैं
terms.everyday_image: नारियल के छिलके के मजबूत रेशे

why_chain.step: पौधे के हिस्सों को मजबूती चाहिए।
मोटी, कड़ी walls सहारा देती हैं; यह waxy बाहरी covering बनाने से अलग काम है।

unpack.consequence: Wall thickness alone cannot identify the tissue described in the stem.
unpack.level_extra: Contrast lignified support walls with epidermal cuticle.

teacher_understanding.question: What does epidermis mean in this plant question?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is the closely fitted outer cell covering that separates underlying plant tissues from the environment.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is its waxy secretion especially relevant?
teacher_understanding.answer: On exposed aerial surfaces such as leaves and young stems, epidermal cells produce materials forming the cuticle.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a plant need this barrier?
teacher_understanding.answer: Exposed surfaces lose water to air. A water-resistant cuticle helps conserve water while the plant remains exposed to sunlight and air.

teacher_understanding.question: How do epidermis and cuticle differ?
teacher_understanding.answer: Epidermis is the cell layer; cuticle is the protective non-cellular covering deposited on its outside. A thicker cuticle does not mean the epidermis is generally the thickest tissue.

items.exam_note: Intended correct option. Do not confuse epidermis, cuticle and suberin.

terms.plain_meaning: पौधे की सबसे बाहर की cell वाली परत
terms.everyday_image: बिस्तर पर बिछी चादर जैसी बाहर की covering

terms.plain_meaning: मोम जैसा पदार्थ जो सतह से पानी निकलना कम करे
terms.everyday_image: मोम लगी सतह पर पानी की बूँद टिकना

why_chain.step: खुली पत्ती से पानी हवा में निकल सकता है।
Epidermis के बाहर की cuticle पानी का निकलना कम करती है।

unpack.example_or_place: Outer surface of a leaf or young stem.
unpack.consequence: Protection reduces surface water loss, but regulated openings are still needed for gas exchange.
unpack.level_extra: The next question supplies the complementary idea: stomata permit exchange through the protective surface.

teacher_understanding.question: What is parenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a simple plant tissue generally made of living cells with relatively thin walls, performing functions such as storage and, in specialised forms, photosynthesis.

teacher_understanding.question: Where can a learner locate it?
teacher_understanding.answer: It occurs in soft plant regions, including much of the fleshy storage tissue of a potato.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does this option not fit the protective surface clue?
teacher_understanding.answer: General parenchyma performs internal functions such as storage; the specialised outer cell covering responsible for the cuticle is epidermis.

items.exam_note: Distinguish general internal living tissue from the protective outer layer.

terms.plain_meaning: जीवित cells वाला सामान्य plant tissue, जो खाना जमा करने जैसे काम करता है

why_chain.step: पौधे को खाना जमा रखने की जगह चाहिए।
Parenchyma की जीवित cells यह काम कर सकती हैं; बाहरी waxy barrier अलग बनावट है।

unpack.consequence: The tissue's function and position eliminate this distractor.
unpack.level_extra: Connect this general tissue to the specialised aerenchyma and chlorenchyma options below.

teacher_understanding.question: What is suberin?
teacher_understanding.answer: Suberin is a water-resistant material deposited in certain plant cell walls, notably cork cell walls; it is not the name of a tissue layer.

teacher_understanding.question: Which familiar association helps distinguish it from epidermis?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cork walls contain suberin, whereas the question's outer epidermal covering is associated with a cuticle containing cutin and waxes.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is suberin a tempting but unsuitable option?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its water-resistant property matches part of the stem, but the question asks for a layer that secretes an outer covering, not the name of a deposited material.

prerequisites: difference between a tissue and a material in its walls
items.exam_note: Category trap: material versus tissue; compare suberin–cork with cuticle–epidermis.

terms.plain_meaning: कुछ plant cell walls में जमा पानी रोकने वाला पदार्थ
terms.everyday_image: बोतल के cork जैसी पानी आसानी से न गुजरने देने वाली बनावट

why_chain.step: कुछ बाहरी plant tissues से पानी का निकलना रोकना जरूरी है।
Cork की walls में suberin जमा होता है, पर पदार्थ का नाम cell layer का नाम नहीं है।

unpack.consequence: A shared protective function does not make suberin interchangeable with epidermis.
unpack.level_extra: Check whether an option names a substance, a tissue or an opening before matching functions.

items.content: Q. Site of gaseous exchange on leaf is:

teacher_understanding.question: What feature must the answer identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: The question asks for the site on a leaf through which gases are exchanged.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does this exchange occur?
teacher_understanding.answer: Primarily through stomatal pores in the leaf epidermis; option b is intended.

teacher_understanding.question: How do gases move through these pores?
teacher_understanding.answer: Gases diffuse along concentration differences between the outside air and internal leaf air spaces. Carbon dioxide can enter for photosynthesis, while oxygen can leave.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the distinction between stomata and guard cells important?
teacher_understanding.answer: Stomatal pores provide the passage, while guard cells regulate its opening. A controller and the opening it controls are not the same structure.

prerequisites: leaves carry out photosynthesis and respiration
items.exam_note: Intended answer: b. The main trap is identifying guard cells instead of the opening.

teacher_understanding.question: What are guard cells?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are specialised epidermal cells surrounding a stomatal pore and regulating its opening.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are guard cells relative to the gas passage?
teacher_understanding.answer: A pair of guard cells borders the pore; gases pass through the opening between them.

teacher_understanding.question: How do they regulate the pore?
teacher_understanding.answer: Changes in their water content and turgor alter their shape, opening or closing the pore.

prerequisites: cells can gain or lose water
items.exam_note: Regulator of the opening, not the intended name of the exchange site.

terms.plain_meaning: पत्ती के छोटे छेद को खोलने-बंद करने वाली दो cells
terms.everyday_image: दरवाजे के दो चलने वाले पल्ले

why_chain.step: पत्ती को gases चाहिए, पर खुला छेद पानी भी बाहर जाने देता है।
Guard cells पानी की मात्रा के साथ आकार बदलकर छेद का खुलना नियंत्रित करती हैं।

unpack.example_or_place: Pair of cells bordering a leaf stomatal pore.
unpack.consequence: Changing pore size affects both gas exchange and water-vapour loss.
unpack.level_extra: Separate opening, surrounding cells and regulatory function.

teacher_understanding.question: What are stomata?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are tiny epidermal openings, each regulated by guard cells, that connect external air with internal leaf air spaces.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are they found on leaves?
teacher_understanding.answer: They occur in the leaf epidermis. Many terrestrial broad leaves have more on the lower surface, but distribution varies.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must a protected leaf surface still have openings?
teacher_understanding.answer: A protective covering limits water loss, but living leaf cells still need gas exchange for photosynthesis and respiration. Regulated pores help balance these needs.

items.exam_note: Intended correct answer; avoid absolute claims that stomata occur only on the lower surface.

terms.plain_meaning: पत्ती की बाहरी परत के छोटे छेद, जिनसे gases अंदर-बाहर जाती हैं
terms.everyday_image: बंद कमरे में हवा आने-जाने की खिड़की

why_chain.step: Protective covering के बावजूद पत्ती को हवा से carbon dioxide चाहिए।
Stomata बाहर की हवा और अंदर की खाली जगहों के बीच रास्ता देते हैं।

unpack.example_or_place: Microscopic openings in a leaf epidermis.
unpack.consequence: Gas exchange also creates a route for water-vapour loss.
unpack.level_extra: Link epidermal protection with controlled exchange; stomata is plural, stoma singular.

teacher_understanding.question: What is aerenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is specialised parenchyma with large air spaces that facilitate internal gas movement and can aid buoyancy in aquatic plants.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is it commonly associated with plant adaptation?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is common in aquatic and waterlogged plants, where internal air spaces help gases reach tissues with limited access to air.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is it not the intended answer despite its connection with gases?
teacher_understanding.answer: It provides internal air spaces, whereas this question asks for the leaf-surface exchange site, which is the stomatal pore.

prerequisites: gases are needed by living plant cells
items.exam_note: Distinguish internal air-space tissue from a surface opening.

terms.plain_meaning: बड़ी हवा वाली खाली जगहों वाला plant tissue
terms.everyday_image: स्पंज के अंदर की खाली जगहें

why_chain.step: पानी में डूबे हिस्सों तक बाहर की हवा आसानी से नहीं पहुँचती।
बड़े अंदरूनी air spaces gases के आने-जाने में मदद करते हैं, पर ये सतह का छेद नहीं हैं।

unpack.example_or_place: Air-space tissue in aquatic plants such as water hyacinth.
unpack.consequence: An air-related function alone does not identify the surface gas-exchange structure.
unpack.level_extra: Remember the structural distinction: internal spaces versus epidermal pore.

teacher_understanding.question: What is chlorenchyma?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is parenchyma containing chloroplasts and specialised for photosynthesis.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is it commonly found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It occurs in green plant parts, including photosynthetic tissue inside leaves.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a photosynthetic tissue not the correct exchange-site answer?
teacher_understanding.answer: It uses carbon dioxide after the gas reaches the tissue; the stomatal pore is the passage across the leaf surface.

items.exam_note: Separate where a gas is used from the opening through which it enters.

terms.plain_meaning: chloroplasts वाला plant tissue जो रोशनी से खाना बनाता है
terms.everyday_image: हरी पत्ती के अंदर खाना बनाने की छोटी रसोई

why_chain.step: पौधे को रोशनी की मदद से खाना बनाना है।
Chloroplasts वाला tissue यह काम करता है; carbon dioxide के प्रवेश का रास्ता stomata हैं।

unpack.example_or_place: Photosynthetic tissue within a green leaf.
unpack.consequence: Gas entry and gas use are related but distinct functions.

items.content: Q. Muscle is connected to bone via:

teacher_understanding.question: What connection is the question asking about?
teacher_understanding.answer: It asks which structure joins muscle to bone.

teacher_understanding.question: Which structure supplies that attachment?
teacher_understanding.answer: A tendon attaches muscle to bone; option b is intended.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this connection produce movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: When a muscle contracts, its pull is transmitted through the tendon to the bone, helping move the bone at a joint.

teacher_understanding.question: How is this different from a ligament's connection?
teacher_understanding.answer: A tendon transmits muscle pull to bone; a ligament connects bone to bone and helps stabilise a joint.

items.exam_note: Intended answer: b. Tendon versus ligament is a standard function-matching trap.

teacher_understanding.question: What is a ligament?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a strong connective-tissue band joining bone to bone and helping stabilise a joint.

teacher_understanding.question: Where can this role be recognised?
teacher_understanding.answer: Ligaments around the knee and ankle help hold the bones in appropriate relation during movement.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does a joint need ligaments rather than unrestricted movement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Bones must move while remaining aligned; ligaments restrain excessive movement and help prevent instability.

prerequisites: a joint is where bones meet
items.exam_note: Bone–bone, not muscle–bone; ligament injuries are commonly associated with sprains.

terms.plain_meaning: एक bone को दूसरी bone से जोड़कर joint को संभालने वाली मजबूत पट्टी
terms.everyday_image: दो हिस्सों को साथ रखने वाला मजबूत strap

why_chain.step: चलते समय joint की bones को अपनी जगह के संबंध में रहना चाहिए।
Ligaments उन्हें जोड़कर जरूरत से ज्यादा खिसकना रोकने में मदद करते हैं।

unpack.example_or_place: Ligaments stabilising the knee or ankle.
unpack.consequence: Ligament damage can make a joint unstable; this differs from losing a muscle's pulling connection.
unpack.level_extra: Match ligament to bone–bone and tendon to muscle–bone.

teacher_understanding.question: What is a tendon?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a strong fibrous connective-tissue structure that attaches muscle to bone and transmits pulling force.

teacher_understanding.question: What familiar body example shows this attachment?
teacher_understanding.answer: The Achilles tendon connects the calf muscles to the heel bone.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a tendon help when someone stands on tiptoe?
teacher_understanding.answer: Contracting calf muscles pull through the Achilles tendon on the heel bone, helping raise the heel.

items.exam_note: Intended correct answer. Understand force transmission instead of memorising just the two connected parts.

terms.plain_meaning: muscle का खिंचाव bone तक पहुँचाने वाली मजबूत डोरी जैसी बनावट
terms.everyday_image: रस्सी खींचने पर उससे बँधा हिस्सा हिलना

why_chain.step: Muscle के सिकुड़ने से bone तभी हिलेगी जब खिंचाव उस तक पहुँचे।
Tendon muscle को bone से जोड़कर यह खिंचाव पहुँचाता है।

unpack.example_or_place: Achilles tendon behind the ankle, joining calf muscles to the heel bone.
unpack.consequence: Damage to this connection can impair movement produced by the attached muscle.
unpack.level_extra: Use a three-part chain: muscle contracts → tendon transmits pull → bone moves.

teacher_understanding.question: What is cartilage?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a firm but flexible connective tissue providing support and, at many joints, a smooth load-bearing surface.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are familiar examples found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is found in the external ear and nose and over bone ends in many movable joints.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does cartilage at bone ends not make it the muscle attachment answer?
teacher_understanding.answer: Articular cartilage helps distribute loads and reduce friction between moving bone surfaces; transmitting muscle pull to bone is the tendon's role.

prerequisites: bones move against one another at joints
items.exam_note: Support and low-friction joint surfaces differ from muscle–bone attachment.

terms.plain_meaning: कड़ा लेकिन कुछ लचीला connective tissue, जो सहारा देता है और कई joints में bone की सतह ढकता है
terms.everyday_image: कान का ऊपरी हिस्सा दबने पर फिर आकार लेना

why_chain.step: Joint में हिलती bone की सतहों पर भार पड़ता है और रगड़ हो सकती है।
Cartilage चिकनी सहारा देने वाली सतह बनाता है; muscle की खींचने वाली डोरी tendon है।

unpack.example_or_place: External ear and articular surfaces of the knee.
unpack.consequence: Location near a joint does not mean every connective tissue there has the same function.
unpack.level_extra: Three-way distinction: tendon transmits pull, ligament stabilises, cartilage supports and smooths joint surfaces.

teacher_understanding.question: What would choosing 'None' assert here?
teacher_understanding.answer: It would reject ligament, tendon and cartilage as the named muscle–bone connector.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should this option be rejected?
teacher_understanding.answer: Tendon is already listed and correctly names the structure that attaches muscle to bone.

items.exam_note: Eliminate after positively identifying tendon rather than guessing from unfamiliar terminology.

why_chain.step: पहले देखना है कि दिए गए नामों में सही connection मौजूद है या नहीं।
Tendon सही connection है, इसलिए 'None' नहीं चुनना है।

unpack.consequence: A verified positive match rules out 'None'.
unpack.level_extra: Apply function matching before option elimination.
